extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic/philosophy; advanced undergraduates and philosophers studying reasoning and language
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic standards for beginning the study of logic by examining language: what logic concerns, how far to analyze reasoning, and detailed distinctions among kinds of names and propositions used in inference. Emphasizes practical limits of analysis and the preliminariness of linguistic scrutiny for correct reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Logic as science of operations subservient to estimation of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the science of the operations of the understanding which are subservient to the estimation of evidence: both the process of advancing from known truths to unknown, and all other intellectual operations insofar as auxiliary to this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the operation of Naming, Definition, and Classification. Logic's object is to analyze reasoning/inference and to frame rules or canons for testing whether given evidence suffices to prove a proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of naming, definition, classification within logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming, Definition, and Classification are operations specially instrumental to the estimation of evidence and therefore lie within the province of Logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These linguistic operations help keep evidence and conclusions permanent and readily accessible in memory and marshal facts so we perceive evidence more clearly and judge sufficiency with fewer errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit analytic depth to what is necessary for practical logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to decompose mental operations into ultimate elements beyond the point required for the practical purposes of logic considered as an art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze reasoning only so far as is requisite to ascertain the difference between correct and incorrect performance; further metaphysical or psychological decomposition may be interesting but is unnecessary for logical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to frame rules/canons for testing sufficiency of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: On the foundation of the analysis of reasoning, bring together or frame a set of rules or canons for testing the sufficiency of any given evidence to prove any given proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analytic work is instrumental and paired with the production of practical canons; evaluation of evidence is the end goal of logical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commence logical inquiry with analysis of language
rubrics_metrics.description: An inquiry into language, so far as is needful to guard against the errors to which it gives rise, is a necessary preliminary to the study of logic because reasoning usually takes place by means of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without insight into the signification and purposes of words, learners risk reasoning incorrectly. Language imperfections can confuse and impede thought; therefore remove this source of error first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey propositions to determine what questions can be asked
rubrics_metrics.description: Before inquiring into modes of resolving questions, inquire what questions are conceivable and what inquiries mankind have actually asked—this is best ascertained by a survey and analysis of Propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every possible answerable question must be contained in a proposition; analysis of propositions reveals the forms of inquiry and judgment available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition structure: subject, predicate, copula
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proposition consists of three parts: the Subject (the thing of which something is affirmed or denied), the Predicate (the name denoting that which is affirmed or denied), and the Copula (the sign denoting affirmation or denial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these components is foundational to analyzing propositions and distinguishing kinds of judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief (assertion) presupposes two objects/names
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest act of belief (a proposition that invites assent or denial) brings together at least two names: one object named as subject, and another as predicate (e.g., 'the sun exists' involves 'the sun' and 'existence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One name alone (e.g., 'the sun') does not call for belief; a predication that joins two namable things does. This distinction underpins the analysis of propositional content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat names as names of things (not merely of ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a word to express a belief, consider it the name of the thing itself rather than merely the name of our idea of it; names inform others about the thing referred to, not just about one's mental image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This usage supports talking about physical facts (e.g., 'the sun causes day') rather than about relations between ideas; adopt common usage of names as referring to things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish words that are names from parts of names (categorematic vs syncategorematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words (particles like 'of', inflected cases, adverbs) are not names and cannot stand alone as subjects or predicates — these are syncategorematic. Words that can stand alone as subject or predicate are categorematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which words are full names in a proposition; only categorematic terms function as terms of predication except when words are mentioned as words (suppositio materialis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Many-worded expressions may form a single name determined by predication
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of words can constitute one single categorematic name (many-worded name) when, by predicating of it, only one assertion is made (e.g., 'John Nokes, who was the mayor of the town' functions as one name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether a sequence of words is one name by observing whether predication yields a single assertion; contrast with constructions joined by 'and' which form multiple names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin classification from ordinary language distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by recognizing distinctions made in ordinary language; enumeration from names brings before us all distinctions recognized by all inquirers, which can later be abridged if some prove nonfundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not impose theoretical taxonomy at the outset; use the vocabulary and distinctions of common usage as the initial catalogue to ensure comprehensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish general (common) names from individual (singular) names
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name is capable of being truly affirmed, in the same sense, of each of an indefinite number of things (e.g., 'man'); an individual name is truly affirmed only of a single thing (e.g., 'John').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to understand scope of predicates and to classify names; general names support general propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish collective names from general names
rubrics_metrics.description: A collective name denotes a whole taken together and cannot be predicated of each individual member (e.g., 'the 76th regiment'); a general name may be predicated of each member separately (e.g., 'a soldier').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some names are collective/individual despite denoting many individuals; this affects how predicates apply and how propositions are formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish concrete names (things) from abstract names (attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete names stand for things (e.g., 'John', 'the sea'); abstract names stand for attributes or qualities (e.g., 'whiteness', 'old age').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjectives like 'white' may be used predicatively as names of objects rather than names of the attribute; maintain the distinction between a name of objects and the proper abstract name of the attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary terminological changes that obscure logical distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about modern shifts in terminology (e.g., using 'abstract' to mean any general name) that obscure older, clearer distinctions between classes of names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer historically and logically precise usages (concrete vs abstract, general vs individual) to avoid confusion in logical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic judges inferences from evidence across sciences (including metaphysics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a science (including metaphysics) proceeds by drawing inferences from evidence, logic becomes the judge of whether those inferences are well grounded and what other inferences would be so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the impartial role of logic as a common standard for evaluating inferential validity across different domains of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not carry logical analysis beyond the point where inaccuracies become visible in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The logician should not carry the analysis of reasoning beyond the point at which any inaccuracy would become visible; going further yields little practical value for the art of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve deeper metaphysical or psychological analysis to sciences that investigate human faculties; logic's extension is determined by its necessities as an art.
